title: Government health spending triples, out-of-pocket expenditure falls to 42.7%
summary: National Health Accounts 2023–24 estimates show a 21.5 percentage point decline in the share of out-of-pocket expenditure over a decade, alongside an increase in government spending on healthcare

contentHtml:
National Health Accounts 2023–24 estimates show a 21.5 percentage point decline in the share of out-of-pocket expenditure over a decade, alongside an increase in government spending on healthcare

India’s Government Health Expenditure (GHE) increased more than threefold from ₹1,29,778 crore in 2013-14 to ₹4,14,196 crore in 2023–24, while the share of Out-of-Pocket Expenditure (OOPE) in Total Health Expenditure (THE) declined from 64.2 per cent to 42.7 per cent, according to the National Health Accounts (NHA) Estimates for India 2023–24, released by the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.

The estimates show a reduction of 21.5 percentage points in the share of healthcare expenditure borne directly by households over the decade. The decline continued in 2023–24, with OOPE falling from 43.4 per cent in 2022–23 to 42.7 per cent in 2023–24.

The simultaneous increase in public healthcare financing and decline in the proportion of expenditure borne directly by households reflect changes in India’s healthcare financing pattern.

The findings also highlight the Government’s efforts, under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, to strengthen public healthcare, provide comprehensive primary healthcare, expand financial protection, improve access to essential medicines and diagnostics, and bring healthcare services closer to communities.

Government Health Expenditure rose from ₹1,29,778 crore in 2013-14 to ₹4,14,196 crore in 2023–24, representing a threefold increase. Over the decade, the Government’s share in Total Health Expenditure increased by 14.9 percentage points, registering an increase of nearly 52 per cent.

The increase in Government Health Expenditure has been accompanied by a reduction in the share of household out-of-pocket payments. Per capita Government Health Expenditure also increased from ₹1,042 in 2013-14 to ₹2,959 in 2023–24, representing an increase of approximately 2.8 times.

Government expenditure on primary healthcare reached approximately ₹1.53 lakh crore in 2023–24, according to the NHA estimates. The investment comes alongside the expansion of Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, which provide comprehensive primary healthcare services closer to communities.

These facilities provide services relating to preventive and promotive healthcare, screening for non-communicable diseases, essential medicines, diagnostics and other primary healthcare interventions.

Social Security Expenditure on Health increased from 6 per cent of Total Health Expenditure in 2013-14 to 11 per cent in 2023–24, marking an increase of five percentage points. This includes the contribution of Government-financed health insurance schemes such as Ayushman Bharat – Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB PM-JAY), State-specific health insurance schemes, social health insurance and medical expenditure for government employees.

Private Health Insurance Expenditure also increased from 3.4 per cent of Total Health Expenditure in 2013-14 to 10.2 per cent in 2023–24, reflecting the deepening of health insurance penetration across the country. The increase in private health insurance expenditure, alongside the rise in Government Health Expenditure, provides enhanced financial protection to the public at large.

Several Government initiatives are aimed at improving access to healthcare services, medicines and medical products at affordable costs. These include the Free Drugs and Diagnostics Initiatives, Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme, Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana and Affordable Medicines and Reliable Implants for Treatment (AMRIT) pharmacies.

Ayushman Arogya Mandirs are expanding comprehensive primary healthcare services closer to people’s homes, while Ayushman Bharat – Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana provides eligible beneficiaries with cashless hospitalisation benefits. These initiatives are complemented by pharmaceutical price regulation undertaken by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority.

The National Health Accounts 2023–24 estimates show changes in India’s healthcare financing between 2013-14 and 2023–24, including growth in Government Health Expenditure, an increase in the Government’s share of Total Health Expenditure, a reduction in the share of direct household spending and an increase in social security financing.

Over the decade, the Government’s contribution to healthcare expenditure increased, while the proportion of expenditure borne directly by households declined. The estimates highlight the Government’s efforts towards Universal Health Coverage through public investment, primary healthcare expansion, access to medicines and diagnostics, and financial protection.
